text: Why can no comparison sort do better than O(n log n) in the worst case?
choices: Because any algorithm must read all n elements and then sort them, costing n plus n log n.
k comparisons distinguish at most 2^k orderings, and there are n! of them, so k ≥ log₂(n!) = Θ(n log n).
Because the pivot in quicksort can always be chosen adversarially to force n² behavior.
Because merging two sorted halves requires n comparisons and the recursion is log n deep.
explanation: It is a counting argument, and it constrains every comparison sort that could ever be written — no cleverness helps, because the bound comes from how much information the comparisons can carry. The escape is to stop comparing: counting sort and radix sort are O(n) because they use values as indices, and they work only when the values are constrained. The way past a lower bound is always to change the problem.
